literature.analogue: Gas-phase cross-reactions of oxygenated peroxy radicals from α-pinene ozonolysis, yielding low-volatility organic dimers.
literature.citation: Quantitative constraints on autoxidation and dimer formation from direct probing of monoterpene-derived peroxy radical chemistry
literature.evidence: Speciated RO₂ and gas-phase C16–20 dimer measurements, together with concentration and radical-chemistry perturbations, implicated RO₂ cross-reactions in dimer production.
literature.difference: An o-cresol-derived reaction partner, the identity of the mixed product, immediate complete transfer to stable aerosol and a rate coefficient for lumped G_A and G_C were not established.

reactions.hypothesis: Particle-phase dimer or oligomer formation in alpha-pinene SOA

literature.analogue: Particle-phase addition of a pinene-derived alcohol to a cyclic acylperoxyhemiacetal to form dimer esters in α-pinene SOA.
literature.citation: Particle-phase accretion forms dimer esters in pinene secondary organic aerosol
literature.evidence: Authentic standards established structures of major ester dimers, and experiments located their formation in particles from pinene ozonolysis.
literature.difference: The two reactants have distinct structures despite being represented by one P_A pool. The bulk rate, irreversible retention and fraction of Manchester organic mass converted remain unmeasured.

reactions.hypothesis: Photochemical fragmentation and volatilization of alpha-pinene SOA

literature.analogue: Irradiation of particle-bound peroxides and other chromophores in α-pinene ozonolysis SOA, followed by loss of volatile products.
literature.citation: Direct Photolysis of α-Pinene Ozonolysis Secondary Organic Aerosol: Effect on Particle Mass and Peroxide Content
literature.evidence: Near-UV irradiation of denuded particles depleted organic peroxides; the inferred particle-diameter loss was 0.56% per day under the authors' solar scaling.
literature.difference: The experiment did not measure one fragmentation coefficient for every particle constituent. Its lamp, peroxide abundance and exposure differ from the illuminated Manchester mixture.

reactions.hypothesis: Photochemical volatilization of isoprene-derived organic aerosol

literature.analogue: Near-UV irradiation of isoprene-derived SOA producing gas-phase small oxygenated organics, including formic acid.
literature.citation: Photodegradation of Secondary Organic Aerosol Particles as a Source of Small, Oxygenated Volatile Organic Compounds
literature.evidence: An irradiated film of chamber-generated isoprene ozonolysis SOA emitted low molecular weight oxygenated products measured in the gas stream by PTR-ToF-MS.
literature.difference: Collected material, film thickness, illumination and precursor oxidation conditions differed from suspended Manchester particles. The gas signal assignments and bulk rate are uncertain.

reactions.hypothesis: Reactive uptake of a pinonaldehyde-like vapor onto seed

literature.analogue: Gas-phase pinonaldehyde reacting after uptake on sulfuric acid/ammonium sulfate particles, giving oligomeric particle material.
literature.citation: Reactive uptake of pinonaldehyde on acidic aerosols
literature.evidence: Particle spectra showed fragments heavier than the pinonaldehyde monomer after vapor exposure. Uptake depended strongly on acidity and was absent on neutral ammonium sulfate in the authors' controls.
literature.difference: V_A is an unresolved pool rather than identified pinonaldehyde. Nominally neutral Manchester seed differs from the acidic seed that gave reactive uptake; neither an uptake coefficient nor permanent coating retention transfers directly.

reactions.hypothesis: Ring opening of cresol radical products to volatile carbonyls

literature.analogue: Gas-phase OH oxidation and ring opening of toluene and 1,2,4-trimethylbenzene to glyoxal, methylglyoxal and other oxygenated fragments.
literature.citation: Mechanistic study of the formation of ring-retaining and ring-opening products from the oxidation of aromatic compounds under urban atmospheric conditions
literature.evidence: Product measurements in aromatic photooxidation identified first-generation ring-opening dicarbonyls from these aromatic precursors.
literature.difference: The measured parent aromatics differ from o-cresol, whose oxidation also has strong ring-retaining channels. No o-cresol-specific cleavage yield, delayed reservoir lifetime or conversion of all reactant mass to one oxygenated vapor follows.

reactions.hypothesis: Gas-phase aromatic peroxy radical accretion in cresol oxidation

literature.analogue: Gas-phase radical accretion following toluene OH oxidation, including oxygenated C7 peroxy radicals and C14 dimeric products.
literature.citation: Oxygenated organic molecules produced by low-NOx photooxidation of aromatic compounds: contributions to secondary organic aerosol and steric hindrance
literature.evidence: Gas-phase CIMS detected rapidly forming dimer signals tracking aromatic peroxy radicals. Dimer formulas were consistent with both RO₂ self- and cross-reactions.
literature.difference: The experiments used aromatic hydrocarbon parents under low NOx. They did not establish an o-cresol radical-pair identity, complete retention after condensation or the fitted lumped rate in Manchester.

reactions.hypothesis: Gas-phase accretion of isoprene-derived peroxy radicals

literature.analogue: Two isoprene-derived hydroxyperoxy radicals HO–C₅H₈O₂ form gaseous C₁₀H₁₈O₄ accretion product plus O₂.
literature.citation: First oxidation products from the reaction of hydroxyl radicals with isoprene for pristine environmental conditions
literature.evidence: Direct sampling of products from OH + isoprene identified the C₁₀ accretion product assigned to the first-generation hydroxyperoxy radical self-reaction.
literature.difference: The Manchester lump aggregates many oxidation products and immediately assigns the accretion flux to stable suspended material; the paper measured gaseous products and does not establish that condensed yield or rate.

reactions.hypothesis: Reactive uptake of an isoprene-derived oxygenated vapor (epoxydiol-like)

literature.analogue: Gas-phase isoprene epoxydiol reactive uptake onto sulfate-containing aerosol.
literature.citation: Reactive Uptake of an Isoprene-Derived Epoxydiol to Submicron Aerosol Particles
literature.evidence: Gaston et al. measured over 500-fold greater uptake on ammonium bisulfate than on ammonium sulfate, where the coefficient was at most 10⁻⁴.
literature.difference: V_I is not measured IEPOX, and Manchester supplied nominally neutral sulfate. Acidity, organic coating, available surface and gas-phase precursor abundance control whether uptake contributes.

reactions.hypothesis: Further gas oxidation of pinonaldehyde-like vapor to condensable products

literature.analogue: Gas-phase pinonaldehyde + OH generates organic products that form secondary aerosol.
literature.citation: Photo-oxidation of pinonaldehyde at low NOx: from chemistry to organic aerosol formation
literature.evidence: Low-NOx photooxidation of pinonaldehyde in chamber experiments produced measurable SOA; varying the seed and aerosol loading affected the inferred yield.
literature.difference: The fitted vapor pool is not a pinonaldehyde measurement, and the Manchester oxidants, yield, gas-to-particle transfer delay and retained mass need separate constraints.

reactions.hypothesis: Photochemical volatilization of oxidized aromatic aerosol

literature.analogue: Near-UV photodegradation of collected SOA from 1,3,5-trimethylbenzene oxidation, releasing small oxygenated gas products.
literature.citation: Photodegradation of Secondary Organic Aerosol Particles as a Source of Small, Oxygenated Volatile Organic Compounds
literature.evidence: The study detected small volatile oxygenates over irradiated films of chamber SOA, including substituted aromatic precursor systems, and found substantial precursor dependence.
literature.difference: The analogue is methylated-aromatic SOA rather than pure o-cresol SOA. Identical photoproducts, irradiation rate, aerosol morphology and mass loss cannot be assumed.

reactions.hypothesis: Further gas oxidation of cresol-derived phenolics to condensable material

literature.analogue: Gas-phase OH addition to o-cresol-derived 3-methylcatechol and successive phenolics produces more oxygenated toluenes and methylbenzoquinones, some of which enter particles.
literature.citation: Formation of highly oxygenated low-volatility products from cresol oxidation
literature.evidence: CIMS and particle DART-MS detected later-generation oxygenated products from cresol oxidation. Separate 3-methylcatechol oxidation experiments traced the next generation of products.
literature.difference: V_C pools compounds spanning many volatilities and the single irreversible S_C flux omits explicitly oxidant-dependent rates, multiple generations and repartitioning.

reactions.hypothesis: Gas-phase alpha-pinene peroxy radical accretion products

literature.analogue: Gas-phase accretion of two C₁₀H₁₅O₁₀ peroxy radicals from α-pinene ozonolysis to form C₂₀H₃₀O₁₈.
literature.citation: Large Gas-Phase Source of Esters and Other Accretion Products in the Atmosphere
literature.evidence: Gas-phase mass spectrometry with isotope substitutions supported accretion from α-pinene peroxy radicals, including a 20-carbon product retaining the expected exchangeable hydrogens.
literature.difference: The chemical identity and concentration of G_A are unresolved in the fit. A gas-phase accretion product need not immediately or entirely reach suspended particles.

reactions.hypothesis: Condensed-phase oligomerization of isoprene SOA products

literature.analogue: Particle-phase ester formation involving isoprene-derived 2-methylglyceric acid units following methacrolein oxidation at high NOx.
literature.citation: Chemical Composition of Secondary Organic Aerosol Formed from the Photooxidation of Isoprene
literature.evidence: Chamber SOA product analysis linked 2-methylglyceric acid monomer units to ester-linked higher oligomers in the high-NOx pathway.
literature.difference: This supports accretion of particular particle constituents, not conversion of all particle organics at one quadratic rate. Humidity, precursor branching, and the negligible suspended mass in Manchester's isoprene-only controls restrict transfer.

reactions.hypothesis: Reactive uptake of aromatic oxidation carbonyls on aqueous aerosol

literature.analogue: Glyoxal vapor reacts during uptake onto deliquesced aqueous ammonium sulfate particles, including formation of nitrogen-containing condensed products.
literature.citation: Online Speciation of Glyoxal Multiphase Reactions on Deliquesced Ammonium Sulfate Particles
literature.evidence: Simultaneous gas- and particle-phase chemical speciation tracked glyoxal uptake and chemical transformation on sulfate seed at relative humidity at or above about 80%.
literature.difference: The experiment supplied glyoxal directly rather than identifying the o-cresol-derived V_C mixture. Liquid water, reversibility, and the yield of persistent material near 50% RH are unresolved.

reactions.hypothesis: Alpha-pinene radical oxidation yielding pinonaldehyde-like carbonyl vapor

literature.analogue: Gas-phase α-pinene OH oxidation forms pinonaldehyde through its peroxy-radical chemistry and subsequent oxidation or photolysis of hydroxy hydroperoxides.
literature.citation: α-pinene photooxidation under controlled chemical conditions – Part 1: Gas-phase composition in low- and high-NOx environments
literature.evidence: Gas-phase analyses detected pinonaldehyde in controlled α-pinene oxidation; further conversion of hydroperoxide intermediates contributed to the low-NOx total pinonaldehyde yield.
literature.difference: The fitted G_A delay, V_A molecular mixture and yield are bulk parameters; effective formation rates in the mixed-O₃/OH Manchester runs were not measured.

literature.analogue: Sunlight photolysis of gaseous pinonaldehyde to lower-carbon gas products, tested separately from OH oxidation.
literature.citation: Photooxidation of pinonaldehyde at ambient conditions investigated in the atmospheric simulation chamber SAPHIR
literature.evidence: In the OH-scavenged sunlight run the reported formaldehyde yield was 0.18 ± 0.20 and no acetone formation was observed. Pinonaldehyde itself decayed, and the measured gas products tested the proposed fragmentation mechanism.
literature.difference: V_A is an ensemble, and a single effective loss coefficient neglects parent-specific photolysis frequencies, spectrum changes and branching into other products.

reactions.hypothesis: Mixed isoprene and monoterpene peroxy termination to volatile products

literature.analogue: Cross-termination of α-pinene- and isoprene-derived gas-phase peroxy radicals giving C14–15 products at the expense of C19–20 monoterpene dimers.
literature.citation: Molecular understanding of the suppression of new-particle formation by isoprene
literature.evidence: CLOUD experiments measured a shift from C19–20 toward C14–15 dimers and suppressed early particle formation upon adding isoprene, consistent with mixed RO₂ termination.
literature.difference: The C14–15 products can still participate in growth. Treating all material as permanently volatile F_AI is a model end member; Manchester NOx, loading, and suspended seed differ.

reactions.hypothesis: Isoprene peroxy chemistry yielding methyl vinyl ketone or methacrolein-like products

literature.analogue: Gas-phase isoprene hydroxyperoxy radicals reacting under HO₂-dominated conditions produce methyl vinyl ketone and methacrolein.
literature.citation: Production of methyl vinyl ketone and methacrolein via the hydroperoxyl pathway of isoprene oxidation
literature.evidence: Continuous-flow chamber photooxidation and selective reagent-ion measurements distinguished the two C₄ carbonyl products and determined their yields.
literature.difference: The lump G_I combines multiple isomers and fates. Manchester's NO/HO₂ competition, additional fragments and gas product yields are not constrained by the suspended mass data.

literature.analogue: Aqueous guaiacol- and syringol-derived phenoxyl radical coupling through C–C or C–O bonds yields dimers and higher oligomers.
literature.citation: Insights into secondary organic aerosol formed via aqueous-phase reactions of phenolic compounds based on high resolution mass spectrometry
literature.evidence: Mass spectra of organics generated by aqueous phenolic oxidation showed dimer and higher oligomer products consistent with phenoxyl coupling.
literature.difference: The analogue used identifiable methoxyphenols in water. The abundance and reactivity of condensed o-cresol-derived phenolics, particle water content, two-body rate and product persistence in the Manchester experiments remain unverified.
